title: Cerebral Cortex & Deep Brain Pathways: Basal Nuclei Map
description: Explore cerebral cortex and deep brain anatomy, covering six cortical layers, white matter tracts, the corpus callosum, internal capsule, and basal nuclei.
h1: Cerebral Cortex, Basal Nuclei, Internal Capsule and Deep Brain Pathways
blurb: Coronal deep-brain architecture: six-layered neocortex, corpus callosum, internal capsule projection highway, caudate, putamen, globus pallidus, and thalamus.
lead: Beneath the folded gray mantle of the cerebral cortex lies an intricate three-dimensional architecture of white matter highways and deep subcortical nuclei. In this illustrated guide to cerebral cortex and basal ganglia, we examine 20 documented structures—including cortical gray matter, layer i · molecular, layer ii · external granular, layer iii · external pyramidal—linking regional topography, tissue architecture, physiological mechanisms, and clinical reasoning.
overview: Beneath the folded gray mantle of the cerebral cortex lies an intricate three-dimensional architecture of white matter highways and deep subcortical nuclei. Most cerebral neocortex has six microscopic layers, but cortical areas and older hippocampal cortex differ. Beneath cortical gray matter, association fibers link areas within a hemisphere, commissural fibers cross hemispheres and projection fibers connect cortex with deeper structures. The internal capsule carries densely packed motor and sensory pathways between thalamus/basal nuclei. The caudate and putamen form dorsal striatum; globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus and substantia nigra participate in motor circuits. The thalamus relays and modulates most sensory streams and important motor signals. Within the human body, the cerebrum · cortex & deep pathways (Cortex cerebri · substantia alba · nuclei basales) is situated in cerebral hemispheres: cortical ribbon, deep white matter, ventricles and diencephalon, receives arterial perfusion via anterior, middle and posterior cerebral arterial territories; perforators supply deep nuclei, and is innervated by corticospinal, thalamocortical, commissural and association pathways.

Structurally, the cortical gray matter (Substantia grisea corticalis) comprises neuronal cell-body sheet folded into gyri and sulci. Physiologically, the cortical gray matter integrates sensory, motor and association information. The layer I · molecular (Lamina molecularis) is superficial neuropil-rich layer below pia, with relatively few neuronal somata. Physiologically, the layer I · molecular supports horizontal intracortical connections. The layer II · external granular (Lamina granularis externa) is small pyramidal and granule-cell zone. Physiologically, the layer II · external granular governs contributes intracortical signaling. Structurally, the layer III · external pyramidal (Lamina pyramidalis externa) comprises pyramidal neurons send many corticocortical and callosal projections. Physiologically, the layer III · external pyramidal links cortical regions and hemispheres. Structurally, the layer IV · internal granular (Lamina granularis interna) comprises prominent thalamic input layer, particularly in primary sensory cortex. Physiologically, the layer IV · internal granular receives major thalamocortical afferents. The layer V · internal pyramidal (Lamina pyramidalis interna) is large pyramidal cells project to brainstem and spinal cord; Betz cells are an example. Physiologically, the layer V · internal pyramidal provides major descending cortical output.

Clinically, regarding the cortical gray matter, regional cortical lesions give different deficits. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the layer I · molecular, six-layer plan is a template, not identical in every area. In clinical pathology involving the layer II · external granular, cell density varies across sensory and motor cortex. Medical evaluation of the layer III · external pyramidal also notes that white-matter injury can disconnect otherwise intact cortex.

questions.question: What lies beneath the cerebral cortex?
questions.answer: Deep white-matter pathways connect cortical regions with each other and with subcortical structures, while deep gray nuclei and ventricles occupy related spaces.

questions.question: Does every part of the cerebral cortex have six layers?
questions.answer: Most neocortex has six layers, but cortical regions vary, and older cortical areas such as hippocampal cortex have a different laminar organization.

questions.question: What is the cortical gray matter?
questions.answer: Cortical gray matter is the neuronal cell-body layer folded into gyri and sulci on the cerebral surface.

questions.question: Where is cortical layer II located?
questions.answer: Layer II, the external granular layer, lies just beneath the molecular layer of the cerebral cortex and contains small granule and pyramidal cells.

questions.question: What is the function of the layer IV · internal granular?
questions.answer: Layer IV of the cerebral cortex receives major thalamocortical input, especially in primary sensory areas.
